content.text: Body close packed
Face centred cubic
Body centred cubic
Cubic close packed

Count where the atoms sit: at the eight corners only, at the corners plus one at the centre of each face, at the corners plus one in the middle of the cube, or in a hexagonal close-packed arrangement.

Two of the names on the list are two names for the same structure, and that structure has atoms at the centres of the faces as well as at the corners. The hexagonal arrangement is not based on a cube at all, so both of those can be eliminated from a cubic sketch with no face atoms.
C
The sketch shows atoms at the eight corners of a cube with a single atom at the centre of the cell, which is the body centred cubic (BCC) unit cell.

content.text: A simply supported beam is loaded with a force $F$ as shown.

content.alt_text: Simply supported beam with a pin support at $L$ and a roller support at $R$, loaded by a downward inclined force $F$ acting between the supports.

content.text: Which diagram correctly shows the reactions at the supports of the beam?

content.alt_text: Reaction force diagram for option A: a simply supported beam with the applied load F, an inclined reaction at L and a vertical reaction at R.
Reaction force diagram for option B: vertical reaction at L and inclined reaction at R.
Reaction force diagram for option C: inclined reaction at L and vertical reaction at R.
Reaction force diagram for option D: inclined reaction at L and a downward vertical reaction at R.

content.text: Start by identifying what each support can resist. A pin can develop two reaction components, but a roller rests on a smooth surface and can only push perpendicular to that surface.

Then apply $\Sigma F_{x} = 0$ and $\Sigma F_{y} = 0$. Because $F$ is inclined it has a horizontal component as well as a vertical one; the horizontal component can only be resisted at the pin, and both supports must push upwards to balance the vertical component.
A

With no horizontal load applied, the horizontal reaction components must balance to zero, and both supports must react upwards against the applied load. Only diagram A shows a consistent set of upward reactions acting perpendicular to the beam at $L$ and $R$.

content.text: Four points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are plotted in orthogonal projection.

content.alt_text: Third-angle orthographic projection of four points A, B, C and D: a plan view above and an elevation view below, with the third-angle projection symbol beside them.

content.text: How many of the lines joining these points are shown at their true length in the views drawn?

A line is drawn at true length only in the view that is parallel to it. Use the alignment between the plan and the elevation: the two views share one horizontal reference line, so a line that is horizontal in one view is parallel to that view's reference plane.

Work out for each line whether the plan or the elevation should be showing it at true length, then measure the drawn length in that view and compare it with the length implied by the other view - the two agree only if the line is at true length.
B

A line is only drawn at true length in the view that is parallel to it: a line parallel to the horizontal plane is true length in the plan, and a line parallel to the vertical plane is true length in the elevation. So each line has to be tested against the reference line the plan and the elevation share.

In the plan, $BC$ is drawn parallel to that reference line, so $BC$ is parallel to the vertical plane and the elevation is the view that shows it at true length. Measuring the drawing, $BC$ is about 450 units long in the elevation - which matches the true length worked out from the two projections together - but only about 436 units in the plan, so the plan is foreshortened.

$DC$ is horizontal in the elevation, so $DC$ is parallel to the horizontal plane and the plan is the view that shows it at true length: $DC$ measures about 327 units in the plan against a true length of 327, and only about 323 units in the elevation.

$AB$ and $AD$ are inclined to both planes, so each is shortened in both views. $AB$ is about 166 units in the plan and 189 in the elevation against a true length of 232, and $AD$ is about 226 in the plan and 216 in the elevation against a true length of 231.
Exactly two lines are therefore shown at true length - $BC$ in the elevation and $DC$ in the plan - so the answer is 2, option B.

items: 1 mark: selects 2 (option B), identifying BC as the line parallel to the vertical plane (true length in the elevation) and DC as the line parallel to the horizontal plane (true length in the plan), with AB and AD foreshortened in both views

content.text: In which of the following pairs are both electronic components semi-conductors?
Diode and resistor
Diode and transistor
Capacitor and resistor
Capacitor and transistor
Classify each component by the material it is built from. Resistors use resistive films or wire-wound elements and capacitors use dielectric materials; both of those are passive components.

The two items in the correct pair are both active solid-state devices made from silicon or germanium, whose four valence electrons per atom can be promoted into a conduction band - that is what makes them semiconductors.
B
A diode and a transistor are both constructed from semiconductor materials (silicon or germanium). Resistors and capacitors are passive components made from resistive or dielectric materials.

items: 1 mark: selects 'Diode and transistor' (option B)

content.text: In which of the following pairs do the forces oppose each other during level flight?
Lift and drag
Thrust and lift
Drag and thrust
Weight and drag

In level, steady flight the aircraft is not accelerating, so every force must be balanced by another force of the same size acting in the opposite direction. List the four forces with their directions: one acts up, one acts down, one acts forwards and one acts backwards.

Then check each pair: a force that acts along the flight path can only be opposed by the other force along the flight path, while a force perpendicular to the flight path is opposed by the vertical force, not by a fore-aft one.
C
In level, steady flight lift balances weight and thrust balances drag, so drag and thrust act in opposite directions along the flight path.

items: 1 mark: selects 'Drag and thrust' (option C)

content.text: A mild steel test piece is placed under an increasing tensile load. When will this test piece start to permanently deform?
At failure
At the elastic limit
At the plastic limit
At the ultimate tensile strength

On a stress-strain curve for mild steel there are two points to identify: the end of the straight-line region through the origin, and the top of the curve. Decide which of them corresponds to 'the piece no longer returns to its original length when the load is removed'.

Permanent deformation begins where the curve first stops being a straight line. The top of the curve is a much later point and describes the maximum load the piece can carry, not the onset of permanent deformation.
B
Up to the elastic limit the test piece returns to its original length when the load is removed. Beyond the elastic limit it deforms permanently, so permanent deformation begins at the elastic limit.

items: 1 mark: selects 'At the elastic limit' (option B)

content.text: Which aeronautical engineering innovation was investigated in Australia by experimenting with box kites?
Aerofoils
Air brakes
Wing flaps
Wing warping

Think about what Lawrence Hargrave's box kites of the 1870s were built to test: a very light, flat, rigid surface that could generate lift in a wind, so that an engine heavy enough to do useful work could one day be carried aloft.
The other three names are all control devices that appeared decades later, once an aircraft could already generate lift; none of them is the lifting shape itself.
A
Lawrence Hargrave's box kite experiments of the 1870s in Australia used an aerofoil with curved upper and lower surfaces, establishing the lift-producing shape that made powered flight possible.

items: 1 mark: selects 'Aerofoils' (option A)

content.text: A block begins to slide when a ramp is inclined to $24^{\circ}$.

content.alt_text: A rectangular block resting on an inclined ramp with the inclination angle marked $24^{\circ}$ at the base.

content.text: What is the coefficient of friction between the block and the ramp?

At the instant the block is on the point of sliding, the friction force has reached its limiting value $F = \mu N$. The component of the weight down the slope is $W\sin\theta$ and the normal reaction is $N = W\cos\theta$.
Divide those two expressions: the weight cancels out, leaving a single ratio of the two trigonometric functions, so the mass of the block is not needed at all.
C

items: 1 mark: selects 0.45 (option C), using $\mu = \tan\theta$

assets.alt_text: A rectangular block resting on an inclined ramp with the inclination angle marked $24^{\circ}$ at the base.

content.text: Which type of satellite is commonly used to broadcast TV signals?
Low Earth-orbit satellite that orbits over the poles
High Earth-orbit satellite that orbits over the poles
Geostationary satellite that orbits above the equator
Geosynchronous satellite that orbits above the Tropic of Capricorn
For a fixed receiving dish to work without tracking, the satellite must stay in the same place in the sky while the Earth turns beneath it.
That requires an orbit in the Earth's equatorial plane at roughly $35\,786\,\mathrm{km}$, not a polar orbit and not an inclined orbit.
C
A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane at about 35 786 km, remaining fixed above one point on Earth so it can continuously broadcast to a fixed receiving dish.

items: 1 mark: selects 'Geostationary satellite that orbits above the equator' (option C)

content.text: Which of the following stress–strain curves best represents a test result showing true stress and true strain of a thermosoftening polymer?

content.alt_text: Stress-strain graph A: a steep initial rise, a small drop, then a long rising curve with a yield-like feature and rising again.
Stress-strain graph B: a single straight line rising linearly from the origin.
Stress-strain graph C: a curve that rises to a peak and then falls (ductile metal with necking).
Stress-strain graph D: a curve that rises gently at first and then curves upwards, increasing without a yield point.

content.text: First decide whether each curve is a true or an engineering (nominal) curve, because the two differ once the area of the specimen changes.
On a true curve the stress is recalculated on the shrinking area, so a material that draws down keeps getting harder instead of falling away after a peak.
D

A thermosoftening polymer has no yield point and no necking; on a true stress–true strain plot the stress continues to rise with strain because the cross-sectional area decreases. Graph D shows this continuously rising curve.

items: 1 mark: selects graph D, the curve that rises continuously with no yield point or necking

Stress-strain graph D: a curve that rises gently at first and then curves upwards, increasing without a yield point.

content.text: Which aircraft engine incorporates bypass air to create thrust?
Scramjet
Turbojet
Turbofan
Turboprop
Think about which engine type splits the incoming air into two streams: one that enters the combustion core and one that never reaches it.
Propulsive efficiency improves when a large mass of air is accelerated by a large fan, instead of being heated to boost its velocity.
C
A turbofan engine routes part of the intake air around the combustion core; this bypass air is accelerated by the fan and contributes most of the thrust, improving propulsive efficiency.

content.text: A $240\,\mathrm{V}$, $75\,\mathrm{W}$ light globe is replaced with a $240\,\mathrm{V}$, $12\,\mathrm{W}$ LED globe of equivalent brightness. What is the theoretical power saving?
$12\,\mathrm{W}$
$63\,\mathrm{W}$
$87\,\mathrm{W}$
$240\,\mathrm{W}$
A saving is a difference, not a ratio, so subtract one rated power from the other.
Both globes are rated at the same $240\,\mathrm{V}$ supply, so no current, resistance or efficiency calculation is needed.
B

content.text: As the applied load is increased during a compression test, what changes occur to the cross-sectional area and gauge length of a copper specimen?
Cross-sectional area: Increases; Gauge length: Decreases
Cross-sectional area: Decreases; Gauge length: Increases
Cross-sectional area: Increases; Gauge length: Increases
Cross-sectional area: Decreases; Gauge length: Decreases
Ask what the specimen must do to carry the compressive load: it has to spread sideways.
That sideways movement is the lateral strain, and Poisson's ratio links it to the axial strain that shortens the gauge length, so the two quantities move in opposite senses.
A

Under compression the specimen bulges sideways, so the cross-sectional area increases, while the gauge length shortens. Poisson's ratio links the two effects, and the true stress rises as the area grows.

items: 1 mark: selects option A, cross-sectional area increases while gauge length decreases

Stored key B is correct, but the stored solution is not: it simplifies the circuit to $Q = A \cdot B$. In fact $Q = \overline{A\cdot B} \cdot \overline{A+B} = \overline{A \cdot B + A + B} = \overline{A+B}$, i.e. $Q = A'B'$, not $AB$. The key is unaffected because both printed rows have one input high, which forces $Q = 0$ either way. Solution left unchanged because it is not in this path's todo.
Solution corrected. The stored equation read Q = overline(overline(A.B)).overline(overline(A+B)) = (A.B)(A+B) = A.B, i.e. it unwrapped the NAND and NOR bubbles into a plain AND, dropping the NOR output from the product. Verified the figure (assets/eng2016_q15_logic_circuit.png): A and B both feed a NAND and a NOR, and the two gate outputs feed a final AND. Correct reduction is Q = overline(A.B) x overline(A+B) = overline(A+B). Key B unaffected — it is the only table giving Q = 0 for both printed rows — and the stored criterion already names table B for 1 of 1 marks, so neither was changed.

content.text: Consider the logic circuit shown.

content.alt_text: Logic circuit: inputs A and B feed a NAND gate and a NOR gate, whose outputs feed a final AND gate to produce output Q.

content.text: Which table shows the correct output values at Q for the given input values A and B?
Work gate by gate for one row of the table: write the output of each gate for that input pair, then combine the two gate outputs at the final gate.

A NAND feeding an AND gate is redundant, because the AND with a NOR output forces the result low whenever either input is high. Test each row of the table separately rather than reading the table as a whole.
B

content.latex: Q = \overline{A \cdot B} \times \overline{A + B} = \overline{A \cdot B + A + B} = \overline{A + B}

content.text: Because $A \cdot B + A + B$ reduces to $A + B$, the whole network collapses to a NOR gate on the two inputs: $Q$ is high only when both inputs are 0. Worked row by row, with $A = 0$ and $B = 1$ the NAND gives $\overline{0} = 1$ but the NOR gives $\overline{1} = 0$, so $Q = 1 \times 0 = 0$; with $A = 1$ and $B = 0$ the two gate outputs are identical and $Q = 0$ again.

Only table B shows $Q = 0$ in both printed rows. The stored solution dropped the NOR output and simplified to $A \cdot B$, which is wrong — it happens to give the same two printed rows because both have one input high, which forces the NOR output to 0 either way. Option D is also the complement of B in both rows and option A reads the NAND output alone, so none of them can be right.

items: 1 mark: selects table B, giving $Q = 0$ for both $(A, B) = (0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$

content.text: What process is applied to dried clay for it to obtain the required compressive strength for use as a common brick?
Annealing
Extrusion
Glazing
Vitrification
Clay only develops compressive strength and weather resistance after it has been fired, so the question is asking what happens to the material during that heat treatment.
Look for the process in which the fired body partly turns glassy and the particles become bonded together by a glassy cement.
D

Firing dried clay bricks to about 1000 degrees Celsius partially vitrifies the clay, forming a glassy cement that bonds the particles and gives the brick its compressive strength and weather resistance.

items: 1 mark: selects 'Vitrification' (option D)

content.text: The diagram shows three pulleys $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.

content.alt_text: Belt and pulley system: pulley X of radius 175 mm driven at 150 rpm, driving pulley Y of radius 350 mm, which is keyed to a second pulley of radius 200 mm that drives pulley Z of radius 100 mm.

content.text: If pulley $X$ rotates at $150\,\mathrm{rpm}$ clockwise, what will be the speed and direction of rotation of pulley $Z$?
$150\,\mathrm{rpm}$ clockwise
$300\,\mathrm{rpm}$ clockwise
$75\,\mathrm{rpm}$ anticlockwise
$150\,\mathrm{rpm}$ anticlockwise
On a belt drive the belt speed is the same at every pulley, and the belt speed is $\omega r$, so compare $n \times r$ from stage to stage.
There are two belts in this drive and each one reverses the direction of rotation, so count the reversals before committing to clockwise or anticlockwise.
A

The belt speed is constant, so $\omega r$ is equal at each pulley. $\omega_Y = 150 \times \frac{175}{350} = 75\,\mathrm{rpm}$ anticlockwise, and the second stage gives $\omega_Z = 75 \times \frac{200}{100} = 150\,\mathrm{rpm}$ clockwise, since each open belt reverses the direction of rotation.

items: 1 mark: selects 150 rpm clockwise (option A)

AS 1100 requires material cut by the offset cutting plane to be hatched continuously across the jog, as if the plane were a single straight plane. Only section A hatches the material through the central web between the two offset cuts.

content.text: What is the position of the maximum bending moment?
The bending moment diagram is the integral of the shear force diagram, so the slope of the moment diagram is the shear force.
The moment therefore stops rising and starts falling at the point where the shear force changes sign, so find the zero crossing on the diagram.
B
The rate of change of bending moment equals the shear force. The bending moment is therefore at its maximum where the shear force diagram crosses zero, which occurs at $B$.

Part (a) is about the seating system itself — how modular construction changes where and how the work is done, why steel is used with concrete, and one tension test. Part (b) is a materials selection justification.
For the Young's Modulus calculation, stress and strain must both come from the same proof load, and the strain is measured over the original gauge length, not the extended length.

content.text: Manufacturers of student travel cards use a PVC based polymer.

content.alt_text: A rectangular plastic student travel pass with rounded corners printed with the words 'Travel pass' and 'school'.

content.text: Justify why a PVC based polymer is a suitable material for this application.
A justification means property, then why that property suits this job — a travel card is carried in pockets and bags, dropped, sat on, and handled by thousands of students.
Think about how a PVC card is actually made: a flat, printed, cheap, mass-produced sheet, and what that implies about the material and the process.

items: Durable and waterproof, so the card survives being carried, rained on and cleaned, and it will not corrode or delaminate.
Very cheap per unit, because PVC is readily mass produced and calendered into flat sheet, which suits a card issued to every student.
When plasticised it keeps enough rigidity to hold its printed face and any chip, while retaining some flexibility, so it is less likely to shatter; it is also light and easily coloured.

content.text: PVC is a durable and waterproof material. It is very suitable for mass production, resulting in low cost per unit, and when plasticised is durable at room temperature, providing appropriate rigidity while retaining some flexibility, reducing the potential for accidental breakage. It can also be calendered to incorporate a chip or image, easily coloured, and is lightweight.

items: 3 marks: Complete and accurate response: identifies an appropriate property of PVC for the application, e.g. it is durable, waterproof or lightweight; shows some understanding of the reasons for using PVC in this application, e.g. low cost per unit from mass production; and justifies the use of PVC by explaining appropriate properties, e.g. rigidity with retained flexibility reduces accidental breakage

2 marks: Partly correct response: identifies an appropriate property of PVC for the application, e.g. it is durable, waterproof or lightweight; and shows some understanding of the reasons for using PVC in this application, e.g. low cost per unit from mass production, but does not address: justifies the use of PVC by explaining appropriate properties, e.g. rigidity with retained flexibility reduces accidental breakage
1 mark: Limited response, addressing only one of the requirements above (e.g. identifies an appropriate property of PVC for the application, e.g. it is durable, waterproof or lightweight)

content.text: Question 22 covers the historical development of communication devices, methods of generating electricity, and a sectioned front view drawn to AS 1100 standards.

Part (a) wants a distinct contribution from each of the three devices, in the order they are shown. Three versions of ‘it improved communication’ score one mark, so identify what new capability each device added — a transmission method, a medium, or a set of functions on one device.
Part (b) needs two genuinely different generation routes, each described as source → conversion device → output. Naming ‘coal’ or ‘solar’ without the mechanism earns only partial credit.

content.text: Describe TWO methods of generating electricity.

Describe each method as a chain: energy source → conversion device → electrical output, and choose two routes that start from different sources, such as a fuel-driven rotating generator and a light-driven or moving-mass-driven one.

Solar photovoltaic cells: visible light → photosensitive diode generating an electric potential → DC collected and inverted for use; no moving parts, but output depends on sunlight and storage is needed at night.

content.text: Explain the benefits of using AS 1100 drawing standards in the preparation of engineering drawings such as the one above.
AS 1100 is a standard for how drawings are made and communicated, so think about the consequences of two people interpreting the same drawing differently.
Standards also decide conventions: Australia projects in first angle while much of the world uses third angle, so a standard removes that ambiguity too.
The question says explain, so attach the benefit to each reason rather than listing reasons on their own.

AS 1100 reduces ambiguity, so the design intent is communicated accurately and the quality of communication between designers, manufacturers and constructors improves. It saves businesses time and money by minimising interpretation errors and rework. Because the standard is based on international (ISO) conventions, drawings can be understood and transferred between countries, and it provides a consistent set of line types, scales and projection conventions for the highway pavement section shown.

The use of AS 1100 standards reduces ambiguity and improves the quality and accuracy of communication between designers and manufacturers. It also allows drawings to be transferred between countries as AS 1100 is based on international standards, and saves businesses time and money by minimising interpretation errors.

content.text: Compare the selection of laminated glass with toughened glass as a windscreen for this vehicle.
This is a comparison of two windscreens for the same job, so treat them in the same order: shared properties first, then the difference in fracture behaviour, then cost, weight and fabrication.
Ask what must not happen when the screen is struck: the driver must not be thrown out and must not be cut by fragments.
Note that does not shatter into dangerous fragments and keeps its shape and stays see-through when cracked are different properties, and each glass type has only one of them.

Both are transparent, hard and scratch resistant, and both are easy to clean. Toughened glass is cheaper and lighter, but when it breaks it shatters into small cubes, so it loses visibility and provides less protection. Laminated glass retains its structural integrity and visual acuity when cracked because the PVB interlayer holds the fragments together, so it is safer; it can also be drilled and shaped at the edges, can carry embedded demister elements, and absorbs more ultraviolet radiation, but it is heavier and more expensive than toughened glass.

Toughened glass and laminated glass are both transparent and hard, which resists scratching from dust and impact of small particles, and both are easy to clean. When broken, toughened glass breaks into small cubes while the laminated windscreen maintains structural integrity and visual acuity. Toughened glass is cheaper to make and lighter; laminated glass can be drilled and shaped at the corners, can embed defrosting elements, absorbs more UV and maintains visibility when fractured.

content.text: Give reasons for selecting an aluminium alloy for the side panel of the truck.
Answer in terms of the loads the panel must carry (its own mass, cargo and any impact) against its cost, and remember that a truck side panel is a large, thin, shaped, exposed surface.
Also consider the environment: the panel is exposed to weather and road splash, and it has to be produced in large flat or curved shapes and attached to the chassis.
The marks want a strength-type property plus a second, unrelated reason — two versions of the same idea is only one mark.

A good strength-to-weight ratio, so the body can be light yet resist impact and deflection; high corrosion resistance, so it does not rust in road salt and weather; easily formed, cut, drilled, bent and fabricated into large panels and bolted or welded to the chassis; waterproof, and it can be painted or anodised; economical compared with steel or composites, and readily recyclable.
Aluminium alloy is chosen for this application as it has a good strength to weight ratio, is easily shaped, waterproof, corrosion resistant and is easy to fabricate and install.

content.text: Truck tyres are made using vulcanised synthetic rubber combined with high tensile steel wire.
Explain why this combination of materials has been chosen.
Do not just list properties. The question asks why the two materials are used together, so the answer must be about what each one does that the other cannot.
Consider the loads on a tyre: vertical load, impact from kerbs and potholes, and the forces that try to squash or spread the sidewall.
Remember what a rubber casing with no reinforcement would do at speed, and what would be lost if the steel were used alone.

Vulcanised rubber is resilient (it absorbs and returns energy), wear resistant, has a high coefficient of friction so it grips the road, and it is formable into the complex carcass and tread. However rubber is very flexible and has negligible stiffness, so on its own it would balloon and distort at speed. The high tensile steel wire has very high tensile strength and stiffness, so it limits that distortion and holds the tyre in shape, while the rubber supplies the grip, resilience and wear-resistant surface.

Rubber has the following properties that make it suited to tyre construction: resilience, wear resistance, formability, and high coefficient of friction. However it is highly flexible and elastic, so it would be too flexible by itself. The high tensile steel band limits distortion of the rubber.

content.text: Aircraft flight control systems use either cables or 'fly-by-wire' systems.
Contrast these flight control systems.
A contrast needs both sides: a feature of one system, the matching or opposing feature of the other, and at least one thing the two have in common.
Trace the path of a single pilot input through each system, from the stick to the control surface, and note every stage that can fail, add mass or add friction.
Think about what each system gives the pilot back: one is immediate, mechanical and tactile; the other is processed, computed and possibly augmented.

items: Similarity: both transmit the pilot's control demand to the control surfaces, and both must be capable of moving the aircraft safely with some form of redundancy.

Cables: direct mechanical linkage from stick to surface, giving immediate force and position feedback to the pilot; simple and independent of any computer, but cables and pulleys add weight and friction, need regular inspection and maintenance, and offer only limited redundancy.

Fly-by-wire: the stick movement is converted to electrical signals, processed by computers and applied to the surfaces by actuators; it removes the weight and maintenance of the mechanical linkage and allows control augmentation, but adds mass for computers, wiring and actuators, depends on electrical power, and introduces the possibility of computer failure.

The pilot must retrain for indirect (fly-by-wire) control, because there is no direct feel of the aerodynamic load and the control response is mediated by software rather than a fixed mechanical ratio.

content.text: Fly-by-wire removes the weight of wires and pulleys and transfers the control functions to computers, with multiple redundancies, but pilots need retraining and computer failure is possible. Cables give a direct connection between pilot and control surface with a direct feedback system to the pilot, but impose physical loads on pilots, need high maintenance of the mechanics such as pulleys and wheels, and offer limited redundancies.

content.text: A taut cable and aerofoil of similar thickness are tested in a wind tunnel. The results show that the aerofoil produces significantly less drag than the cable.

content.alt_text: Wind tunnel test diagram: a circular cable cross-section above and a symmetrical aerofoil section below, with the air flow region left blank for the candidate to complete.

content.text: Explain how the aerofoil produces less drag than the taut cable. Use the diagram to assist your response.
Compare the two bodies the same way: what shape is each one, and what happens to the air immediately behind it?

Drag is set by two things — how much low pressure the body leaves in its wake, and how much friction its surface creates — and both are decided by the shape of the rear of the body and the roughness of its surface.
Annotate the empty flow region of the diagram with streamlines and with the separation and vortex region for each body; that annotated diagram is part of what is being marked.

The circular cable is a bluff, non-aerodynamic body. The air cannot stay attached around its curved rear surface, so it separates early and leaves a large region of low pressure and turbulent eddies behind the cable, and that pressure difference plus skin friction over its rough surface produces a large drag. The aerofoil is streamlined and smooth: the air is guided around it and stays attached for much longer, giving a far smaller wake, less turbulence and much less skin friction, so for the same thickness and frontal area it produces significantly less drag.

The non-aerodynamic shape of the cable creates a low pressure behind it that acts to pull the wire backwards and create significant drag. The cable has a rough surface that generates significant surface drag, and it also generates significant vortices behind it that act to produce drag. The symmetrical aerofoil has a smooth surface and aerodynamic shape that minimises turbulence behind the aerofoil and significantly reduces drag.

items: 3 marks: Explains how each profile affects drag, using the diagram, e.g. the streamlined aerofoil keeps the flow attached and leaves a small low-pressure wake, while the blunt cable causes separation and a large low-pressure wake
2 marks: Explains how one profile affects drag, or uses the diagram to show how drag is affected without comparing both profiles
1 mark: Identifies an appropriate reason, e.g. a low-pressure region behind the body produces drag

content.text: What are redundant truss members?

Define redundancy relative to the load case, not to the member itself: ask what force the member carries for the loading shown, and whether the truss would behave identically with that member removed.
The full mark needs both the zero-force statement and the qualification that a different loading can make the same member load-carrying.

A redundant member is a member that carries no force — a zero-force member — under the loading currently applied, so removing it would not change the forces in the rest of the truss for that load case. It is not permanently redundant: under a different load case the same member may carry load.

A redundant member is a member in a truss that carries no load under current conditions. The load in the truss member may vary under different load conditions, which means it may not necessarily become redundant.

items: 2 marks: Complete and accurate response: identifies a relevant feature of a redundant truss member, e.g. it carries no load under the current loading; and states what a redundant truss member is, noting that it may carry load under a different load case
1 mark: Limited response, addressing only one of the requirements above (e.g. identifies a relevant feature of a redundant truss member, e.g. it carries no load under the current loading)

content.text: The structural steel I-beams used to make the crane were hot-rolled then normalised.
Explain why normalising was chosen as the heat treatment process. Support your answer with a labelled sketch of the resulting microstructure.

Normalising reheats the steel into the austenite range and then cools it in still air, so the cooling rate sits between furnace cooling and quenching. Think about what that does to grain size, and therefore to strength and toughness.

A crane beam has to be strong without becoming brittle or expensive, so the justification is about gaining adequate strength economically and relieving residual stress. The sketch has to show the grain size the process produces, and it must be labelled.

Normalising was chosen because it refines the grain structure, giving an increase in strength through grain size strengthening at lower cost than alloying or quench-and-temper, while leaving the beam ductile, and it relieves the residual stresses left by hot rolling. The resulting microstructure, which the sketch must show, is a fine, uniform structure of small equiaxed grains.

Normalising of a steel beam produces a fine uniform grain structure that produces an increase in strength through grain size strengthening. It is economical when compared to other methods of strengthening, and it relieves stress. The resulting microstructure sketch shows small, evenly sized equiaxed grains.

items: 4 marks: Complete and accurate response: identifies an appropriate reason for normalising, or provides a sketch that represents the resulting microstructure; explains why normalising was chosen as the heat treatment process; provides a labelled sketch that represents the resulting microstructure, e.g. small uniform equiaxed grains; and explains with a labelled sketch why normalising was chosen as the heat treatment process, resulting in a correct microstructure

content.text: The table compares the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions of three transport systems – car, train and aircraft.

columns: Kilograms of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emission per passenger per hour

content.text: Part (a) is not really about emissions at all. It asks why society needs more than one kind of transport, so set the table aside for that part.
For part (a), think about what each mode is good at: distance, speed, how many people can be moved at once, and how close it can get people to where they actually want to go.

For part (b) an innovation only earns full credit when the chain of reasoning is complete: name the innovation, say how it works, say what it changes, and then say what that does to the environment. A named innovation on its own earns very little.

items: 2 marks: part (a) — Why are these different transport systems still required?
7 marks: part (b) — For each transport system shown in the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions table, explain how an engineering innovation in that…

content.text: The table shows that these transport systems produce different amounts of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions per passenger.

columns: Kilograms of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emission per passenger per hour

content.text: Why are these different transport systems still required?
The answer is about choice, not about emissions. No single mode can do everything, so the different systems are each the best option for particular journeys.
One mark is for naming a valid reason and one is for explaining how that reason justifies keeping more than one system. A bare list of reasons earns one mark only.

The systems are still required for convenience (a car goes door to door), for access to a range of passengers including those who cannot drive, for long distance travel, for journey times and for safety. Each mode meets a different need, so the lowest emission mode for one journey is not the best mode for every journey and all three are still required.
These systems are still required for the following reasons: convenience; access to a range of passengers; travelling long distances; journey times; and safety.

items: 2 marks: Complete and accurate response: identifies a relevant reason, e.g. convenience, access to a range of passengers, or journey times; and explains how or why different transport systems are still required, e.g. trains serve long distances while cars offer door-to-door convenience
1 mark: Limited response, addressing only one of the requirements above (e.g. identifies a relevant reason, e.g. convenience, access to a range of passengers, or journey times)

content.text: For each transport system shown in the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions table, explain how an engineering innovation in that transport system has affected the environment.
Three transport systems and seven marks means a different, well explained innovation for each. Using the same innovation in all three will not earn three separate explanations.

For each system, complete the chain: the innovation, the mechanism by which it works, the change in fuel or energy use, and the resulting effect on the environment. Marks are given for the explanation, not for the name.
For the aircraft, look at where the thrust actually comes from: a large proportion of the air passing through the engine is never burnt, which is why engine efficiency improved so dramatically.

items: Car: weight reduction using aluminium alloys and carbon fibre composites plus aerodynamic shaping reduce mass and drag, so less fuel is burnt and CO2 emissions per passenger fall.
Train: AC traction with VVVF inverters and regenerative braking replaces DC control that wasted electricity as heat, so less electricity and less diesel fuel is used and emissions fall.
Aircraft: high bypass turbofan engines produce up to about 90% of their thrust from unburnt bypass air, and winglets reduce induced drag, so fuel burn and therefore CO2 emissions per passenger fall.

content.text: Cars: weight reduction using stronger aluminium alloys and carbon fibre composites reduces vehicle mass and therefore fuel consumption, and aerodynamic shapes reduce drag, so the car emits less $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Trains: modern VVVF drives with AC motors instead of DC motors control torque and voltage more efficiently, since DC control wastes electricity as heat, and AC motors allow regenerative braking as the train slows or descends, reducing electricity and diesel fuel use and therefore $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions. Aircraft: turbofan engines optimise the entrainment of bypass air, which produces up to 90% of thrust and dramatically improves fuel efficiency, while winglets and flow control devices minimise wing tip vortices, reducing drag and improving lift so less fuel is burned.

items: 7 marks: Gives a complete explanation of how engineering innovations in all three transport systems have affected the environment
5–6 marks: Gives a sound explanation of how engineering innovations have affected the environment in at least two transport systems
3–4 marks: Gives a sound explanation of one innovation and its environmental effect plus some description of a second, or some description of three innovations
1–2 marks: Identifies an innovation or an environmental impact, or lists characteristics of relevant innovations
